title: A Continuous Murmur Under the Collarbone / Machinery Sound and a Collapsing Pulse

blocks.text: A Continuous Murmur Under the Collarbone / Machinery Sound and a Collapsing Pulse

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-36 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease (Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645), key points summarised by the American College of Cardiology (August 2020) · Related AMaC: AMaC Eisenmenger syndrome, aortic regurgitation and patent ductus arteriosus stations; this one tests the continuous murmur, the collapsing pulse and the pulmonary pressure that decides closure
The patient is a woman of 22, a university student. A murmur has been known since childhood. She is getting more breathless on stairs. Please examine her cardiovascular system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A continuous machinery murmur below the left collarbone with a collapsing pulse in a young adult is a patent ductus arteriosus. The marks come from timing the murmur through both heart sounds, and from asking about the shunt and the pulmonary pressure.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates call it aortic regurgitation and listen at the apex only. Pass: left infraclavicular, continuous, collapsing pulse, shunt, pulmonary pressure. Fail: aortic regurgitation, with no check of the toes.

rows: She is well. Look at her colour, hands, fingers and toes, then feel the pulse and the neck before the chest.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; colour; clubbing; pulse character; blood pressure; neck veins.
Palpate the apex and the left upper chest, then listen below the left collarbone and over the back.
"I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs and ankles."
Apex; thrill; murmur timing; second sound; lung bases; feet and toes; ankles; cover her.
Name the lesion, what the shunt does, and the tests that decide closure.
"She has a patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt. She needs echo and pulmonary pressure assessment."
Present in order; diagnosis; complications; echo; catheter; closure; follow-up; thank her.
Starts without consent; presses hard on the chest; leaves her exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone and stops if she is breathless.
Disorganised; omits the pulse character, the toes or the infraclavicular area.
Looks at hands, colour and neck veins, feels the pulse, palpates apex and thrill, listens below the left clavicle, then bases, toes and ankles.
Also compares fingers with toes and checks the blood pressure for a wide pulse pressure.
Reports a diastolic murmur or cyanosis that are absent.
Finds a collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure, displaced apex and a continuous murmur with a thrill below the left collarbone; pink fingers and toes.
Also finds a loud second sound that would suggest rising pulmonary pressure.
Calls it aortic regurgitation or a venous hum.
Patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt.
Also separates it from a venous hum, an aortopulmonary window and a coronary arteriovenous fistula.
Names left heart volume overload, pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, with differential cyanosis, and endocarditis; asks for ECG, echo and chest X-ray.
Also asks for the degree of left ventricular volume overload and a calculated pulmonary vascular resistance by echo and catheter.
Calls a cyanosed or deteriorating patient well, or sends her away with no pulmonary pressure assessment.
Says closure is considered when the shunt causes left ventricular volume overload and pulmonary vascular resistance is low, and follow-up continues.
Also gives the resistance bands for closure and says high resistance needs an expert-centre decision.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: well; respiratory rate 14; pulse 88 collapsing; blood pressure 132/48; SpO2 98% on air in fingers and toes; temperature 36.6 °C. No clubbing, no cyanosis. Apex displaced, hyperdynamic. A thrill and a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle, loudest at the end of systole. Second sound normal. Lung bases clear. No oedema.

Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B, R3) Collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure, displaced apex, thrill and continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle, pink fingers and toes. 2. Diagnosis? (D, R4) Patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt. 3. What is the differential? (D, R4) Aortic regurgitation, venous hum, aortopulmonary window, coronary arteriovenous fistula. 4. Which tests? (E, R5) ECG, chest X-ray, echo; left ventricular volume overload and pulmonary vascular resistance. 5. When is closure considered? (E, R6) Left ventricular volume overload from the shunt with pulmonary vascular resistance below 3 Wood units (Class I); 3 to 5 (Class IIa); above 5 an expert-centre decision (ESC 2020).

Curveballs: She asks if she can run: advice from the congenital team. She has blue toes but pink fingers: reversed shunt, urgent referral. She asks about pregnancy: assessment by the congenital team first.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about pain (G)
Checks the pulse character, blood pressure and toes (A)
Palpates the apex and listens below the left clavicle (A)
Finds a collapsing pulse and a wide pulse pressure (B)
Finds a continuous machinery murmur and thrill (B)
Names patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt (D)
Separates it from aortic regurgitation and a venous hum (D)
Lists pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger syndrome and endocarditis (E)
Requests echo and pulmonary vascular resistance (E)
Covers her, cleans hands and thanks her (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the apex only.) [R2 Fail] Cyanosis and a diastolic murmur. [R3 Fail] Aortic regurgitation. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Heart failure. [R5 Fail] She is well, so nothing more is needed. [R6 Fail]
Examiner note: Pulmonary pressure decides treatment, and a missed reversal of the shunt is dangerous. No consent, the infraclavicular area skipped, and the lesion misnamed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, colour, pulse, neck veins; apex; thrill; below the left clavicle; bases, toes and ankles.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: She has a collapsing pulse, a wide pulse pressure and a continuous machinery murmur with a thrill below the left collarbone, with pink fingers and toes. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A patent ductus arteriosus. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, endocarditis. ECG, echo and chest X-ray. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Closure is considered by the left ventricular volume overload and the pulmonary resistance, with lifelong follow-up. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not name the differential, the resistance bands or the expert-centre decision.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, may I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll stop if you're breathless. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, fingers and toes, pulse volume, blood pressure; apex; thrill; below the clavicle; bases; ankles.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Collapsing pulse, pulse pressure about 84, displaced apex, continuous murmur with thrill, normal second sound, pink toes. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A patent ductus arteriosus, not aortic regurgitation, a venous hum, an aortopulmonary window or a coronary fistula, because the murmur is continuous. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Tests?
CANDIDATE: ECG, echo, chest X-ray; the left ventricular volume overload and pulmonary vascular resistance by echo and catheter. Differential cyanosis would mean a reversed shunt. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Close when the shunt overloads the left ventricle and resistance is below 3 Wood units; 3 to 5 should be considered; above 5 needs an expert centre. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands, thanks her.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, the pulse pressure, the differential, differential cyanosis and the closure bands.
R2: Listening only at the apex. The murmur is below the left collarbone.
R4: Calling it aortic regurgitation. That murmur is diastolic; this one is continuous.
R5: Naming heart failure alone. Pulmonary hypertension decides whether closure is safe.
R6: Calling her well and stopping. Pulmonary resistance must be assessed before any closure decision, and a reversed shunt would be missed.
"May I listen below the left collarbone and feel for a thrill?"
"The murmur is continuous with a collapsing pulse, so I'd say a patent ductus."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Patent ductus arteriosus: a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle, a collapsing pulse and a wide pulse pressure. A left-to-right shunt overloads the left heart, and rising pulmonary pressure can reverse it (Eisenmenger syndrome, with toes blue and fingers pink).

ESC 2020 (closure thresholds as summarised by the ACC): with a left-to-right shunt that causes left ventricular volume overload, closure is Class I if pulmonary vascular resistance is below 3 Wood units, Class IIa for 3 to 5, and Class IIb above 5, a careful individual decision in an expert centre. Closure is not appropriate once the shunt has reversed (Eisenmenger physiology). Pulmonary vascular resistance is measured at right heart catheterisation, not estimated from the murmur.
Endocarditis is a recognised risk of an unclosed ductus; lifelong follow-up at a congenital heart disease service.
THINK: Continuous murmur, collapsing pulse: PDA.
SAY: "A persisting channel between the aorta and the pulmonary artery."
DO: Pulse character; below the clavicle; check the toes.
NUMBERS: Left ventricular volume overload; resistance below 3 Wood units (ESC 2020, Eur Heart J 2021).
TRAP: Aortic regurgitation; apex only.
FINISH: Echo, resistance, closure decision, follow-up.
